blocks.title: Addition polymerisation
blocks.text: In addition polymerisation, monomers add to each other one by one, forming long chains. All the atoms of the monomers become part of the polymer; nothing is lost and no side product such as water forms.

The monomers must have a C=C (or C triple bond C) bond, which opens up to let the monomers link together. The process is often a chain reaction started by a very reactive molecule, an initiator, which forms free radicals. For example, many ethene molecules join end to end: n CH2=CH2 -> [-CH2-CH2-]n (initiator, heat, pressure), where n is very large, up to about 10 000.

blocks.alt: Top: n CH2=CH2 with an initiator, heat and pressure gives poly(ethene), drawn as a bracketed -CH2-CH2- unit with subscript n. Bottom: n CH2=CHCl gives part of a PVC chain, six carbons with Cl on every second carbon; repeat unit -CH2-CHCl-.
blocks.caption: Addition polymerisation of ethene and chloroethene (original diagram after the book's equations).
blocks.long_description: In each case the double bond of the monomer becomes a single bond in the chain and the monomers join end to end. The polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer, because no atoms are lost.

blocks.text: Poly(ethene) is mainly of two types. Low density poly(ethene) (LDPE) is used where a very light, soft material is needed, such as shopping bags and light plastic bottles. High density poly(ethene) (HDPE) is made from ethene at low pressure and temperature with a Ziegler-Natta catalyst and is used for plastic containers, thick shopping bags and toys. LDPE chains are more branched, so they cannot pack tightly, giving a less solid, more elastic material; HDPE chains are linear and pack closely, giving a tough, dense structure.

blocks.alt: Left: LDPE, zigzag chains with side branches, loosely packed. Right: HDPE, straight zigzag chains lying close together.
blocks.caption: Branched LDPE and linear HDPE chains (original sketch for this topic).
blocks.long_description: Side branches keep LDPE chains apart, so the forces between them are weaker and the plastic is soft and of low density. Unbranched HDPE chains lie side by side, so the forces between them are stronger and the plastic is denser and tougher.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Ziegler-Natta catalysts are a Nobel Prize-winning invention that changed plastic production. Karl Ziegler discovered them in 1953; they made the low-pressure polymerisation of ethene into linear HDPE possible, and Giulio Natta extended them to stereoregular polymers such as crystalline polypropene.

PVC is made from chloroethene by addition polymerisation: n CH2=CHCl -> [-CH2-CHCl-]n. Its properties can be changed a lot by adding plasticisers, chemicals that make materials softer, more flexible and easier to work with, by reducing the strong forces between polymer chains. Rigid PVC (without plasticisers) is hard and stiff, chemically inert to most acids, bases and oils, a good electrical insulator, naturally resistant to burning (self-extinguishing) because of its chlorine atoms, and long-lasting. Plasticised PVC is flexible and soft and can be bent and shaped easily, while keeping good chemical and electrical properties.

items: Pipes and fittings for water supply, drainage and sewage, because it resists corrosion and lasts.
Window frames, door profiles and vinyl floor tiles and sheets.
Electrical insulation for wires and cables.
Cling films, bottles (e.g. for cooking oil) and blister packs.
Raincoats, artificial leather and inflatable products such as swimming pools.

blocks.prompt: Why does adding a plasticiser make PVC flexible?
blocks.explanation: Plasticiser molecules get between the polymer chains and reduce the strong forces between them, so the chains can move past each other more freely.

items: Addition: C=C monomers join; nothing lost; initiator starts a chain reaction.
LDPE branched and soft; HDPE linear and tough (Ziegler-Natta).
PVC: rigid or plasticised; pipes, insulation, medical tubing.
